title: Joel 3:1–8
context: Joel 3:1–8 opens the last chapter of the book. Versification: English 2:28–32 is Hebrew 3:1–5, and English chapter 3 is Hebrew chapter 4; this page keeps the WEB numbers. The LORD speaks throughout these verses. The opening words “in those days, and in that time” tie the oracle to what comes just before it, the promise of the Spirit poured out and the word that “whoever will call on the LORD’s name shall be saved” (2:32; see the Romans 10:13 box, with Acts 2 named in its own setting). When the LORD restores the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem, he will gather all nations into “the valley of Jehoshaphat” and execute judgment on them for scattering his people, dividing his land, and trading in captives (3:1–3). The name Jehoshaphat means the LORD judges, and the place is not otherwise known. A later tradition identifies it with the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem, some readers recall King Jehoshaphat’s victory in 2 Chronicles 20, where the place of blessing is named “Beracah Valley”, and many take the name as symbolic, matching “the valley of decision” in 3:14. None of these identifications is certain. Verses 4–8 turn to Tyre, Sidon, and all the regions of Philistia, charged with taking the LORD’s silver and gold and selling the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks; the LORD promises to return their repayment on their own heads and to have their own children sold to the men of Sheba. Amos 1:6–10 brings a similar charge of trading captives against Gaza and Tyre, and Ezekiel 27:13 lists Javan among the traders of Tyre who “traded the persons of men”. Joel’s date is debated, and these details are sometimes used in that discussion without settling it; the exact occasions behind the charges are uncertain. Historical, typological, and future readings of the valley and of the day of the LORD are held by readers in both traditions, and these notes present them side by side without choosing among them. Shared ground: the LORD remembers his scattered people and judges those who wronged them.

verses.text: “For, behold, in those days, and in that time, when I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD sets the judgment of the nations inside his promise to restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem. Arminian readers stress that this restoration follows the call to return in 2:12–14 and the promise to all who call on the LORD’s name in 2:32, so the scene of judgment stands beside a real offer of mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read “when I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem” as the LORD’s own initiative in keeping his covenant with his people. They see the judgment of the nations as the other side of that same faithfulness, and with Arminian readers they place the restoration and the judgment in the same day.

verses.text: I will gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat; and I will execute judgment on them there for my people, and for my heritage, Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations. They have divided my land,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD gathers all nations to the valley of Jehoshaphat, a name meaning the LORD judges, and gives his reasons: they scattered his people and divided his land. Arminian readers note that the charges are specific deeds, so the judgment answers what the nations have actually done rather than an arbitrary sentence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD calls Israel “my people” and “my heritage”, and they read the judgment as God defending what belongs to him. Both traditions hold historical, typological, and future readings of the valley, and its location, whether the Kidron or a symbolic name, is uncertain.

verses.text: and have cast lots for my people, and have given a boy for a prostitute, and sold a girl for wine, that they may drink.
verses.arminianNotes: The verse describes captives treated as cheap goods: lots cast for the people, a boy given for a prostitute, a girl sold for wine. Arminian readers see God’s anger at contempt shown to human beings made in his image, and they read the coming judgment as just recompense for real cruelty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same contempt and stress that the LORD counts wrongs done to his people as done against himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as an indictment of war and the trade in captives, and both see the LORD as defender of the helpless.

verses.text: “Yes, and what are you to me, Tyre and Sidon, and all the regions of Philistia? Will you repay me? And if you repay me, I will swiftly and speedily return your repayment on your own head.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD turns to Tyre, Sidon, and the regions of Philistia and asks whether they mean to repay him. Arminian readers hear a measure-for-measure principle like Obadiah 15, “As you have done, it will be done to you.” They see accountability for nations that thought themselves beyond reach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the swift and speedy return of repayment “on your own head” and read it as the certainty of God’s justice. They observe that the exact occasion behind the charges against these coastal peoples is uncertain, and that Amos 1:6–10 brings a related charge without fixing a date.

verses.text: Because you have taken my silver and my gold, and have carried my finest treasures into your temples,
verses.arminianNotes: The charge is that Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia took the LORD’s silver and gold and carried his finest treasures into their temples. Arminian readers note that the LORD calls the plunder his own, and they hear a warning that taking what belongs to God is sacrilege as well as theft.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read “my silver and my gold” as the LORD’s claim of ownership over all that was taken from his people and his house, compare Haggai 2:8. Which plunder is meant is not stated, and both traditions treat any link to a specific raid as uncertain.

verses.text: and have sold the children of Judah and the children of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, that you may remove them far from their border.
verses.arminianNotes: The people of Judah and Jerusalem were sold to the sons of the Greeks and removed far from their border. Arminian readers see the cruelty of forced exile for profit, and they hear the LORD taking up the cause of the scattered, in keeping with his concern for the oppressed throughout the prophets.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same cruelty and note that Ezekiel 27:13 lists Javan among the traders of Tyre who “traded the persons of men”. Readers differ on what the mention of Greeks implies about the date of Joel, and both traditions leave that question open rather than building doctrine on it.

verses.text: Behold, I will stir them up out of the place where you have sold them, and will return your repayment on your own head;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises to stir up the captives from the places where they were sold and to return the repayment on the sellers’ heads. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness reaching people scattered far away, and they read the reversal as a pledge that no one is beyond his notice or his care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the LORD himself does the stirring, so the return of the captives rests on his power and promise rather than on the strength of the scattered. Both traditions see the verse as part of the restoration promised in 3:1 and leave the historical fulfillment of its details uncertain.

verses.text: and I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hands of the children of Judah, and they will sell them to the men of Sheba, to a faraway nation, for the LORD has spoken it.”
verses.arminianNotes: The sellers become the sold: the LORD will sell their sons and daughters into the hands of Judah, who will sell them to the men of Sheba, a faraway nation. Arminian readers read this as poetic justice announced against Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia, and they acknowledge how hard the image is for readers today.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the closing words, “for the LORD has spoken it”, as the seal of certainty on the sentence. The Sabeans of Sheba are commonly placed in southern Arabia as a trading people, though details are uncertain, and both traditions read the verse as retribution, not as approval of slavery.
